title: Rearrange a formula to isolate a named variable
aliases: make the subject of the formula
applies: The target variable is named. Other symbols are treated as given parameters unless the problem says otherwise.
steps: Mark the target and collect its terms on one side.
Undo operations in reverse order, or factor out the target if it appears in several terms.
Record parameter restrictions before dividing, rooting, or applying another inverse operation. Handle excluded cases separately if requested.
pitfalls: A coefficient might be zero for some parameter values.
Even powers can have multiple inverse branches over the reals.
checks: Substitute the rearranged expression into the original formula on its stated domain.

example.problem: Make r the subject of P=2πr+h.
example.answer: Subtract h and divide by 2π to get r=(P−h)/(2π).

title: Find a percent of an amount or recover the base
applies: The percent is measured against a specified base or whole.
steps: Identify the part, whole, and percentage. Convert p% to p/100.
Use part=(p/100)×whole and solve for the missing quantity.
Check for zero before dividing by the base or percentage.
pitfalls: The whole is the reference amount. A percentage increase or decrease can use a different reference from the part.
checks: The part and whole use the same units. Recompute the part from the reported whole and percentage.

title: Test complex differentiability with the Cauchy–Riemann equations
applies: The input is complex and you can express the real and imaginary parts in real coordinates.
steps: Write z=x+iy and separate u and v.
Compute the four first partial derivatives.
Find where both Cauchy–Riemann equalities hold. Verify continuous partials nearby for the standard sufficient test at a point.
If they hold throughout an open region with continuous partials, f is holomorphic there and f′=u_x+i v_x.
pitfalls: Equalities at a point without the required regularity are insufficient.
Differentiability at an isolated point does not imply holomorphy in a neighborhood.
checks: Check both equalities and the open domain. When in doubt, compare difference quotients from independent directions.

example.answer: Nowhere. u=x²−y²+x and v=2xy−y, so u_x=2x+1 differs from v_y=2x−1 everywhere.

title: Evaluate a contour integral by residues
applies: The integrand is meromorphic on the region used by the contour and has no singularity on the path.
steps: Locate and classify the isolated singularities.
Determine which poles have nonzero winding number and use the contour orientation.
For a simple pole at a, compute lim(z→a)(z−a)f(z). For a higher pole, extract the (z−a)^−1 Laurent coefficient.
Sum the weighted residues and multiply by 2πi.
pitfalls: A pole on the path needs separate treatment.
A clockwise contour reverses the sign.
checks: Mark the included poles explicitly and compare the result with partial fractions or Cauchy's integral formula where available.

example.problem: Integrate 1/[z(z−2)] around the counterclockwise unit circle.
example.answer: Only z=0 lies inside. Its residue is −1/2, so the integral is −πi.

title: Choose a branch of a complex logarithm
applies: z is nonzero and the task asks for logarithm values or a continuous branch on a specified domain.
steps: Write z=re^{iθ} with r>0.
Give all values by adding 2πk to θ unless a branch is prescribed.
For one branch, select a continuous argument on the allowed domain. On the standard principal slit plane use −π<Arg(z)<π.
pitfalls: The point zero has no logarithm.
The analytic principal branch excludes the nonpositive real axis.
Logarithm product identities can differ by multiples of 2πi.
checks: Exponentiate the reported value and verify the chosen argument lies in the branch range.

title: Expand a function in a Laurent series on an annulus
applies: The center and requested annulus are known, and the function is analytic throughout that annulus.
steps: Locate singularities relative to the center and split rational expressions into simpler factors if helpful.
For each factor, choose the geometric ratio whose modulus is below one on the specified annulus.
Expand and collect powers of z−z₀. Record the annulus with the final series.
pitfalls: Different annuli around the same center can yield different expansions.
A geometric expansion requires |ratio|<1.
checks: Multiply a simple factor back into the expansion and verify the leading terms and convergence radius.

title: Compute Fourier sine and cosine coefficients
pattern: Period 2L: a_n=(1/L)∫_{−L}^L f(x)cos(nπx/L)dx; b_n uses sin
applies: The interval defines one period and the function is integrable there. Standard pointwise convergence claims require additional regularity.
steps: Identify the period 2L and choose the matching frequency nπ/L.
Find a₀ and the sine and cosine coefficients. Use symmetry to remove vanishing terms.
Write a₀/2+Σ[a_n cos(nπx/L)+b_n sin(nπx/L)]. For a piecewise smooth periodic function, use the average of the one-sided values at jumps.
pitfalls: The constant term is a₀/2 with this convention.
The periodic extension may jump at the interval endpoints.
checks: Check parity, normalization, and one coefficient directly from its defining integral.

example.problem: Find the sine coefficients for the 2π-periodic extension of f(x)=x on (−π,π).
example.answer: The function is odd, so all cosine coefficients vanish. Integration by parts gives b_n=2(−1)^{n+1}/n.

title: Use Parseval's identity to compute mean square or energy
pattern: Mean square = a₀²/4 + (1/2)Σ_{n≥1}(a_n²+b_n²) for a real 2L-periodic function
applies: A real square-integrable periodic function has sine/cosine coefficients in the stated convention.
steps: Identify the Fourier convention and the interval length.
Square coefficients and sum with the constant and harmonic factors.
Multiply by the period for integrated energy, or take a square root for root mean square.
pitfalls: Use the constant factor for your coefficient convention.
Energy, mean square, and RMS differ by the period or a square root.
checks: For a finite series, integrate its square directly and use orthogonality to verify cross terms vanish.

example.problem: Find the RMS of sin x+2cos(2x) over one period.
example.answer: The mean square is (1²+2²)/2=5/2, so the RMS is √(5/2).

title: Compute continuous convolution by tracking overlap
applies: The integral exists. For compactly supported functions, the moving overlap determines its limits.
steps: Find where f(s) and g(t−s) are simultaneously nonzero.
Split the t-axis at points where an overlap endpoint changes.
Integrate the product over the appropriate overlap on each interval and give the result piecewise.
pitfalls: Reflect and shift g as g(t−s), preserving its original support conditions.
A fixed integration range can overcount at the overlap boundaries.
checks: Verify the output support and use commutativity or the integral-of-convolution identity when applicable.

example.problem: Convolve two unit-height pulses supported on [−1/2,1/2].
example.answer: The overlap has length max(1−|t|,0), which is the convolution.

title: Interpolate through distinct nodes with Lagrange polynomials
applies: The x-coordinates are distinct, and you need the unique polynomial of degree at most the number of nodes minus one.
steps: For each node, construct its basis polynomial that is one at that node and zero at all the others.
Weight each basis polynomial by its observed y-value and sum.
Evaluate directly or use the barycentric form for repeated numerical evaluation.
pitfalls: Repeated nodes need a different interpolation setup, such as Hermite conditions.
A high-degree fit can oscillate, particularly near or beyond the nodes.
checks: Substitute every node to recover its original value. Separate interpolation from extrapolation.

example.answer: The polynomial is x²+1, which hits all three points. Its value at 3/2 is 13/4.

title: Find a maximum network flow and certify it with a cut
pattern: 0≤f(e)≤capacity(e), conservation at all nonterminal vertices, max flow=min cut
applies: A directed network gives nonnegative capacities and distinct source and sink vertices.
steps: Start with zero flow and construct the residual network with reverse edges.
Find a residual source-to-sink path and augment by its smallest residual capacity.
Repeat until no augmenting path remains. BFS path selection yields Edmonds–Karp.
Use vertices still reachable from the source as one side of a minimum cut.
pitfalls: Reverse residual edges allow earlier decisions to be corrected.
A cut sums original capacities from the source side toward the sink side.
checks: Verify capacity limits and conservation, then show the flow value equals the cut capacity.

example.problem: Edges s→a, s→b, a→b, a→t, b→t have capacities 3,2,1,2,3. Find max flow.
example.answer: Send 2 via s→a→t, 2 via s→b→t, and 1 via s→a→b→t. The source cut has capacity 5, certifying a maximum of 5.
